w: Opened in 1909 as the Helios under German rule, it kept projecting films in the same small room through war, border changes and every technology shift since. Guinness World Records certifies it as the oldest continuously operating cinema on the planet. Velvet seats, one screen, still run by locals in the old town.
s: Guinness-certified oldest running cinema, since 1909
why: Guinness World Record holder: oldest continuously operating cinema on Earth

w: Built in 1911 in Vienna's Margareten district, this single-screen hall kept its curved art deco walls and copper ticket counter through a century of ownership changes. Now an arthouse cinema showing restored prints and festival premieres, it remains one of the city's last unaltered early-cinema interiors.
s: 1911 art deco cinema with a copper ticket counter
why: one of Vienna's last intact early-cinema interiors

w: Opened in 1924 as Bal Negre by Martinican brothers, this Montparnasse dance hall drew Josephine Baker, Hemingway and Cocteau to hear Antillean rhythms and early jazz. Renamed Le Bal Blomet, it still books live sets nightly and is often cited as continental Europe's oldest continuously running jazz venue.
s: Montparnasse dance hall since 1924, Bal Negre roots
why: claimed to be Europe's oldest continuously operating jazz venue

w: Housed in a low brick cellar beneath the old Delphi cinema on Kantstrasse, Quasimodo has booked touring jazz, blues and soul acts since the 1970s, becoming one of West Berlin's few basement clubs to survive the Cold War years intact. Small stage, packed tables, still running nightly sets.
s: Jazz cellar under the old Delphi cinema, since 1970s
why: one of Berlin's longest-running jazz basements, unchanged since the wall years

w: Founded in 1948 by radio host Luis Villas-Boas, this cramped stone cellar off Praca da Alegria is widely called continental Europe's oldest jazz club. A 2009 fire gutted the room, but musicians and regulars helped rebuild it, and decades of nightly sets have continued in the same tiny space ever since.
s: Basement jazz club since 1948, Europe's oldest claim
why: widely cited as the oldest jazz club in continental Europe

w: Set inside a crumbling 1880s brick warehouse in Almagro, La Catedral turns into one of the city's most bohemian milongas after dark, its walls hung with murals and secondhand furniture under a high wood-beamed roof. Beginners and veterans share the same worn floor for nightly tango classes and dancing.
s: Milonga inside an 1880s grain warehouse in Almagro
why: raw, underground milonga in a 19th-century warehouse, a Buenos Aires institution

w: Built by Fela Kuti's children as spiritual successor to his original Shrine club, the New Afrika Shrine in Ikeja keeps Afrobeat alive with free weekly sets from Femi and Seun Kuti before crowds that treat the open-air hall as sacred ground. Portraits and shrine-like decor tie it directly back to the genre's birthplace.
s: Rebuilt home of Fela Kuti's Afrobeat, still nightly
why: living heart of Afrobeat, direct successor to Fela Kuti's original club

w: Opened in 1909 inside the Lucerna Palace built by Vaclav Havel's grandfather, this grand hall was the first cinema in Prague to show sound film and remains the country's oldest continuously operating one. The 453-seat auditorium still hosts festival premieres and gala screenings beneath ornate Art Nouveau plasterwork.
s: 1909 Art Nouveau palace cinema, Czechia's oldest
why: oldest continuously running cinema in the Czech Republic

w: Opened in 2003 inside Beirut's Starco Center, MusicHall staged multilingual, multi-genre cabaret nights through the city's hardest years, mixing Arabic, French, Armenian and Kurdish acts on the same bill under founder Michel Elefteriades. Al Jazeera called it the place where the heart of world fusion music beats.
s: Cabaret-style venue fusing Beirut's mixed cultures
why: wartime-era cabaret venue that fused Beirut's mixed musical cultures onstage

w: Financed personally by King Rama VII and opened in 1933 at the edge of old Bangkok, Sala Chalermkrung was Southeast Asia's most modern theatre of its day, built with a hydraulic orchestra pit and no columns to block sightlines. It now hosts khon masked-dance shows weekly inside its original art deco shell.
s: 1933 royal art deco theatre financed by the king
why: royally financed 1930s theatre, an architectural landmark of old Bangkok

w: Opened in 1933 in Yokohama's rough portside Noge district, Chigusa was bombed out in 1945, rebuilt its record collection through the occupation years, closed again in 2007, then was resurrected in 2012 by devoted regulars near its original spot. Vinyl still spins in the room that helped seed Japan's postwar jazz culture.
s: Japan's oldest jazz cafe, revived twice since 1933
why: Japan's oldest surviving jazz cafe, saved by community effort more than once

w: Owner Sugawara Seiji converted an earthen family warehouse in provincial Ichinoseki into a jazz-listening room in 1970, naming it for Count Basie. The bandleader heard of the tribute and visited in 1980, arriving by wheelchair up ramps Sugawara built specially. Fans still travel far for its reputedly unrivaled acoustics.
s: Remote jazz kissa Count Basie himself once visited
why: obscure rural jazz kissa its namesake, Count Basie, actually visited in person

w: First opened in 1913 on Birger Jarlsgatan, Zita has cycled through lives as a silent-film house, part of a large chain empire and briefly an adult cinema before settling into its current role showing independent and world film. It remains Stockholm's oldest cinema still screening under its original name.
s: Stockholm's oldest running cinema, open since 1913
why: Stockholm's oldest cinema still operating under its original name

w: Opened in 1909 as the Olympia on Kluuvikatu, Maxim has operated continuously at the same central Helsinki address for over a century, making it Finland's oldest cinema. The original hall, designed by David Frolander-Ulf, still screens films behind a modest facade a short walk from Senate Square.
s: Finland's oldest cinema, same address since 1909
why: Finland's oldest cinema, unchanged address for over a century

w: Built in 1828 in the convict-era Rocks district, the Fortune of War claims the title of Sydney's oldest continuously licensed pub. Sandstone walls and a low timber ceiling frame a stage that still hosts live bands most nights, carrying on nearly two centuries of drinking and music inside the same room.
s: Sydney's oldest licensed pub, live music since 1828
why: Sydney's oldest continuously licensed pub, still hosting live bands nightly

w: Trading as a hotel since 1859 in Geelong, the Barwon Club has run live music almost continuously for more than 165 years, one of the longest unbroken entertainment runs of any venue in Australia. Local and touring rock, blues and folk acts still fill its band room most weekends.
s: Live music in the same pub, unbroken since 1859
why: one of Australia's longest continuously running live-music pubs

w: Built as the ballroom of the Hotel Palace on Copenhagen's City Hall Square, Grand Teatret has screened films almost without interruption since the early 1910s, making it one of Europe's longest-running cinemas. Ornate plasterwork from its ballroom days still crowns the digitised modern screens below.
s: Cinema inside a 1910s hotel ballroom, still screening
why: century-old cinema still housed in its original hotel ballroom shell

w: Opened in 1947 by Haitian immigrant Joseph Walcott, Wally's was the first African-American-owned nightclub in New England and remains Boston's longest continuously running jazz club. Berklee students have jammed alongside veterans on its tiny stage for generations, in a South End room barely changed since opening.
s: First Black-owned nightclub in New England, since 1947
why: New England's first Black-owned nightclub, still a nightly jazz jam

w: Opened in 1976 near Itaewon, All That Jazz became the launchpad for South Korea's jazz scene and is considered the country's oldest jazz club, holding concerts nearly every night of the year. It moved to a new red-lit room nearby in 2023 but kept its original name and its role as ground zero for Korean jazz musicians.
s: South Korea's oldest jazz club, running since 1976
why: birthplace and elder statesman of South Korea's entire jazz scene

w: Opened in 1939 in Marianao's wooded outskirts, Tropicana built its reputation on open-air stages set among mature trees, feathered showgirl costumes and Havana's biggest dance orchestras. It survived the revolution as a state-run spectacle and still stages nightly cabaret shows largely unchanged from its pre-1959 glamour.
s: Open-air 1939 cabaret, showgirls under the trees
why: pre-revolution open-air cabaret still staging its original spectacle nightly

w: Set inside a converted colonial-era warehouse in Lapa's antiques district, Rio Scenarium stacks three floors of chandeliers, gramophones and vintage furniture around a central samba stage and dance floor. The clutter of found objects doubles as a props store for a rental business, giving the club a genuinely lived-in, museum-like feel.
s: Samba club inside a three-floor antiques warehouse
why: samba club that doubles as a three-story antiques museum

w: Opened in 1948 just off Istanbul's Istiklal Avenue, Atlas Sinemasi is one of the last surviving single-screen halls from the golden age of Beyoglu's cinema row. Closed and threatened for years, it was restored by Turkey's Ministry of Culture between 2019 and 2021 and reopened with its original marquee and auditorium intact.
s: 1948 cinema on Istiklal, restored by the state
why: restored survivor of Beyoglu's vanished golden-age cinema row

w: Opened in 1938 overlooking Tangier's Grand Socco, this art deco cinema anchored the city's international-era film culture through decades of Spanish and Moroccan ownership. Restored in 2006 by artist Yto Barrada as North Africa's first cinematheque and archive, its swirling red-and-blue facade still marks the entrance to the old medina.
s: 1938 art deco cinema turned film archive on the Socco
why: art deco cinema turned North Africa's first film archive

w: Inaugurated in 1911 for King George V and completed the following year, this baroque hall is India's last surviving opera house, staging European opera, Marathi theatre and silent films through Bombay's golden decades. It closed in 1993 and sat derelict for 23 years until a meticulous restoration reopened it in 2016 for concerts and events.
s: India's only surviving opera house, reopened 2016
why: India's only surviving opera house, saved by a 23-year restoration

w: Designed by Laszlo Hudec and opened in 1933 on Nanjing Road, the Grand Theatre introduced Shanghai to air conditioning, simultaneous foreign-film translation and the city's first wide screen beneath its distinctive lotus-shaped roof. Still operating today, it keeps a floor of archival photos tracing its run as old Shanghai's premier cinema.
s: 1933 lotus-roofed art deco cinema, still running
why: Shanghai's oldest running cinema, an architectural icon of 1930s modernity

w: Built in 1923 on a plot once known as Palacio de las Pipas, this modernist hall fell dark in the 1960s before Madrid's city council restored it and reopened it in 1989 as Cine Dore, seat of the Filmoteca Espanola. It remains the city's oldest surviving cinema building, now dedicated to classic and restored film screenings.
s: 1923 cinema, now home to Spain's national film archive
why: Madrid's oldest surviving cinema, now the national film archive's home

w: Opened in 1939 on what is now Talaat Harb Street, Cinema Metro was designed by an American architect for MGM's Cairo premieres and became Egypt's first air-conditioned movie theatre. Its art deco facade and vertical marquee still anchor downtown Cairo's cinema row from the city's mid-century golden age.
s: 1939 art deco cinema, Egypt's first air-conditioned
why: Egypt's first air-conditioned cinema, a downtown art deco landmark

w: Opened in 1920 by a Greek hairdresser inspired by his years in Paris, Cine Paris relocated in the 1960s to a fifth-floor rooftop in Plaka, where films now screen with the floodlit Acropolis looming overhead. A four-year restoration by the Stelios Philanthropic Foundation reopened it in 2024, keeping Athens's most scenic open-air screen alive.
s: Rooftop open-air cinema under the Acropolis since 1920
why: rooftop open-air cinema screening films beneath the floodlit Acropolis
